macro: The October Beige Book paints a picture of modest to moderate growth across most Federal Reserve Districts, with manufacturing outpacing consumer spending. Overall employment levels showed little to no net change, with some firms reducing headcount through attrition or delaying hiring. Persistent uncertainty around energy prices and tariffs is weighing on the economic outlook, with most Districts expecting only slight growth ahead.
rates_fed: Inflation commentary in the Beige Book is net negative, with Iran-linked elevated energy prices bleeding into the broader economy — a dynamic that was also visible in this morning's CPI release. Four Districts reported an acceleration in the pace of price increases since the prior period, and higher oil prices permeated all twelve District reports. Wage pressures are also building as workers demand cost-of-living adjustments and benefit costs rise.
market_outlook: The Beige Book leans bearish on the inflation and margin front. The combination of sticky input cost pressures, energy pass-through via fuel surcharges, and consumer resistance to further price hikes is squeezing corporate margins and complicating the Fed's path. The key catalyst to watch is how markets digest this morning's CPI print alongside the Beige Book's corroborating stagflationary undertones.
bull_case: Nine of twelve Districts reported at least modest economic growth, suggesting the expansion remains intact and recession risk is not imminent. Firms across most Districts maintained a positive economic outlook for coming months. Manufacturing activity appears to be holding up as a pillar of growth even as the consumer softens.
bear_case: Inflation is re-accelerating at the input level, with energy prices from Iran-linked supply disruptions now visibly spreading through supply chains via diesel costs and fuel surcharges. Consumer-facing firms are seeing margin compression as price-sensitive shoppers resist further hikes. Four Districts reported a pickup in the pace of price increases, and firms expect more inflation ahead as existing contracts expire and hedges must be renegotiated.
sectors: Manufacturing is outperforming consumer-facing sectors. Consumer discretionary and retail face margin pressure as customers resist price increases. Energy sector dynamics are driving broad input cost inflation across transportation and supply chain-dependent industries. Tourism is growing but showing softness tied to a decline in Canadian visitors in Boston, Minneapolis, and San Francisco Districts. AI investment is suppressing job creation in some firms, which has implications for staffing and HR-related sectors.
key_dates: Oct 14 — CPI released earlier this morning
tts_summary: Here's your midday update for October 14th. The Fed just released the October Beige Book, and the takeaway is not a comfortable one for markets. The report is broadly consistent with what recent data has been telling us — decent but slowing growth, muted job creation, and inflation that is proving stubborn and is now picking up steam in ways that should concern investors and policymakers alike. Let's break it down. On growth, nine of the twelve Federal Reserve Districts reported at least slight to moderate expansion. Manufacturing is the engine right now — consumer spending is largely flat across most Districts. Tourism is growing, though there's a notable softness tied to fewer Canadian tourists visiting Boston, Minneapolis, and San Francisco. Companies are also investing in AI to boost productivity, which is allowing some firms to reduce headcount through attrition and delay hiring — so the labor market cooling is partly structural, not just cyclical. Now here's the part that matters most for markets today. Inflation is the problem. Iran-linked elevated energy prices are no longer contained to the pump — they are bleeding through the entire supply chain via elevated diesel costs and fuel surcharges. That dynamic was visible in this morning's CPI print, and the Beige Book confirms it is broad-based. Four Districts reported that the pace of price increases actually accelerated since the last report. Three Districts called overall price growth robust. Eight said moderate, but three of those flagged intensifying input pressures. Firms expect more inflation ahead as existing contracts roll off and they are forced to renegotiate both input hedges and delivery contracts at much higher prices. On top of energy, tariffs, commodities, and insurance costs are all adding to the pressure. Meanwhile, consumer-facing businesses are absorbing more of those costs because their customers are pushing back on further price hikes — meaning margins are getting squeezed from both sides. Wages are also moving higher, not just from tight labor markets but because workers are explicitly demanding cost-of-living adjustments. The net read here is stagflationary. Growth is modest at best, inflation is sticky and potentially reaccelerating, and corporate margins are under pressure. That is a difficult backdrop for equities and gives the Fed very little room to pivot toward easier policy. Stay cautious into the close and watch for any Fed speak that responds to today's dual inflation signals from CPI and the Beige Book.
